posts.headline: Chief Technology Officer @ Biddano | Technology Management, Technology Leadership
posts.text: These days, building a software product has become fast, but building it right is a much bigger challenge.While building one of my products, I was bombarded with information from my AI agent. At that point, I had two options: blindly accept its suggestions or take the time to understand the information not just the code. I believe this ability will become a key hiring criterion: processing large amounts of information, applying judgment, and using that context to solve real-world problems. This is where strong analytical thinking will matter.Future interviews may focus less on DSA and more on your ability to understand complex context and make sound decisions. Those who master this skill will have a significant advantage in the tech industry. But how do you master it? From my experience, engineers now need domain expertise alongside technical skills. Engineers need to understand the broader business problem instead of thinking only at the API level. Memorising API endpoints and payloads adds little value. What matters is understanding the use cases and functionality of each API and module. You also need a strong mental model of the database structure and the relationships between its entities. When AI asks you to accept or reject a change, your judgment depends on how well you understand both the system and the business.The challenge is that AI can create hundreds of database tables in 30 minutes, but understanding and validating them takes much longer. Engineers are working with a system that can generate solutions faster than they can review them, while still lacking crucial context about the actual business problem. People working in tech need to develop these skills. Otherwise, a fresher with strong contextual understanding and judgment could deliver more value than an experienced developer. Even as IITs face placement challenges today, I believe demand for top talent will rise sharply again over the next two years with significantly higher compensation. The definition of “top talent,” however, is changing.

posts.text: You may be too small to have your own internal platform team. That’s not the same as being too small for platform engineering. If you’re a small engineering team, you don’t need a platform department. You don't need a platform product manager, a portal with forty plugins, or a team maintaining abstractions nobody asked for. That would be ridiculous, and anyone pitching it to you at that size would need a very specific reason that explains why. The question I'd ask instead is what your engineers keep doing repeatedly that you could solve once. That answer is usually concrete. Every team writing CI pipelines from scratch. The same infrastructure provisioned slightly differently each time. Setting up a test VM or DB or Cluster and spinning it down after testing. Operations that depend on one person's memory or knowledge. Everyone, including software developers, needing to know the same handful of Terraform or Kubernetes commands. Outdated Knowledge Based in Confluence. None of that needs a department. It needs a few reusable capabilities and someone who owns them. And it is very possible I once consulted for a startup where I was the only DevOps engineer supporting more than 20 engineers. No platform team. Still a platform. Automated paths and self-service, built so developers could handle their own operations without coming to me. If your engineers can already deploy, provision what they need and understand their own services without waiting on anyone, don’t build a platform because someone told you to. You’re fine. But as the product grows, so does the platform underneath it, and more of this becomes necessary. That still doesn’t mean hiring a team. The goal is to remove enough repeated work that you don’t need one yet. Which of those is costing your engineers the most time right now? #PlatformEngineering #DevOps #EngineeringLeadership

posts.text: AI just moved from “interesting tool” to “institutional priority.” In one week, we saw government rebrand AI in legal contexts as “super intelligence,” OpenAI publish math benchmark progress that’s shaking up parts of research, universities launch new AI degrees, healthcare pilots expand AI prescribing, and companies keep redirecting budgets from headcount to automation. Why this matters: For engineers and technical professionals, this is no longer just about model capabilities. It’s about how AI is being embedded into law, education, medicine, hiring, and capital allocation. The technical stack is becoming organizational strategy. 3 key takeaways: • AI is becoming a systems-level decision, not a side project The White House and DOJ signals suggest AI is being framed not just as software, but as a national capability with legal and policy implications. That changes procurement, governance, and the expectations placed on technical teams. • Frontier model progress is getting more domain-specific and harder to ignore OpenAI’s math results are drawing attention because mathematics is a proxy for reasoning, abstraction, and research assistance. Whether or not you buy the hype, engineers should expect stronger AI support in formal problem-solving, coding, verification, and scientific workflows. • The labor market is being reshaped unevenly Georgia Tech launching an online AI master’s reflects rising demand for AI skills. At the same time, Reuters reports companies are cutting jobs as investment shifts toward AI. The signal is clear: teams that can integrate, evaluate, and govern AI will likely gain leverage; teams that can’t may face compression. The bigger pattern: AI adoption is no longer constrained by model availability. It’s constrained by trust, safety guarantees, regulation, and whether organizations can turn prototypes into reliable production systems. Question for the audience: What will matter most over the next 2 years for technical professionals: • Building with AI • Evaluating and governing AI • Deep domain expertise that AI can augment • Something else entirely?
